title: The Rooftop Nibbler
markdown:
Gadzooks, but Saturday was the best day on the roofs! Rafi the apprentice and Bit the jackdaw treated it as gospel: after a week of hauling buckets and hammering nails, they earned a picnic on the tallest building in town, the one that tickled clouds.

Rafi was a young lad with bright, curious eyes and hands as steady as the foundations he helped build. He climbed to their usual spot, a wide sunny ledge at the tippy-top. Bit, his sharp-witted, glossy-feathered sidekick, was already there, preening with a proud little flourish, as if he owned the weather. “Caw! Caw!” he said, which, if you spoke jackdaw (and Rafi did, oh yes), meant, “Is it ready yet? My beak is watering!”

Rafi grinned, heart as sturdy as a well-set ridge. He pulled a bright red-and-white checkered blanket from his worn leather satchel. “Patience, my feathered friend! Cheese-and-pickle sandwiches, the kind that make a tummy rumble, a crispy apple that shines like a ruby, and — wait for it — a whole jam tart.” He patted the bag. “Enough for two, and a few extra crumbs for you, of course.”

They spread the magnificent feast. The sun, a giant golden coin, warmed their faces. The city buzzed far below like a sleepy bumblebee, its noises muffled by height. Rafi took a huge happy bite of sandwich. Cheesy goodness stretched just a little. He set it down for a second to reach his cool fizzy lemonade.

A corner was gone. Not a big chunk. Not a messy tear. A perfect, tiny, impossibly neat, bite-sized nibble.

“Hey!” Rafi frowned, surprised. Bit hopped closer, beady black eyes missing nothing, head tilted so one eye asked, Who did that? He scanned the ledge. No snooping cats. No stray dogs. Not even a particularly bold pigeon looking for handouts.

Rafi chuckled, a sound like pebbles tumbling down a drainpipe, which is a very roofer-like chuckle. “Must have been a bit windy,” he said, though he knew in his bones that was not quite right. The air was still and soft. He picked up the sandwich, took another delicious bite, and set it down more carefully this time.

Whoosh. Another tiny nibble vanished — this time from the bright red apple. A neat little crescent, gone in a flash, leaving a perfectly smooth edge.

Bit let out a series of quick, questioning caws that sounded suspiciously like, “Did you see that? A magic sandwich! Where did it go?” He had seen something, or rather he had seen nothing happen, and the food was still disappearing. A culinary vanishing act.

“Right.” Rafi straightened. His roofer’s brain, so good at tricky angles and loose tiles, kicked into a different kind of construction. A rooftop puzzle. “We need a plan.”

“The tart is the main event,” he said. The jam bubbled like a tiny volcano. “If a nibbler is working, they will come for that.”

Bit puffed. “Caw, caw, caw.” Lead on.

Rafi tapped his chin. He did not want only to shoo the thief. He wanted a name, or at least a face. A loose tile sat at the roof’s lip, begging to be nudged. From his pocket he took a smooth grey pebble the size of a pea.

“A roofer’s special,” he whispered. He crowned the tart with the pebble and eased the tile until it wobbled on the edge. “When they reach, they bump the tile. The pebble rolls. Clatter. We know where they are.”

They scurried behind a sturdy red-brick chimney, a cozy hideaway, and peeked with all their might, eyes like twin telescopes. City sounds faded to a distant hum. They waited. Hearts ticked.

A tiny rustle, almost lost in the breeze. Then a quick furtive movement near the blanket. A small furry head popped up, whiskers twitching like antennae. A squirrel! Cheeky-looking, bright curious eyes darting.

Bold as brass, it hopped onto the checkered cloth. Delicate paws reached for the jam tart, nose busy with sugar. Just as tiny fingers brushed the golden crust, it bumped the wobbly tile.

Clatter! The tile tipped with a surprising noise. The pebble rolled and landed with a distinct thud. The squirrel froze, fur on end, utterly startled. It looked at the pebble, then at the tart, then up at the chimney. Caught red-pawed.

Rafi could not help a delighted chuckle. Bit let out a triumphant, echoing caw-caw-CAW. The squirrel looked rather sheepish. It did not scamper away in a panic. It sat, a little guilty and a little hungry, bushy tail twitching as if trying to decide whether to be a flag or a broom.

They stepped out slowly, faces a mixture of surprise and amusement. “Well now, Mr. Cheeky-Cheeks,” Rafi said, voice soft and kind. “You have been sneaking our lunch.”

The squirrel chittered a series of squeaks that seemed to mean, But it smelled so good, and I was so hungry. Bit, ever the understanding friend, hopped forward and nudged a small piece of sandwich crust toward it. “Caw?” Here. Have some. We understand.

The squirrel sniffed, whiskers quivering, then gobbled. Its tail gave a happy grateful flick.

Rafi smiled until his eyes crinkled. “You know what, Bit? This is much better than catching a thief. We have enough for a friend.” He broke off sandwich and a chunk of apple. “Here you go, little nibbler. Plenty for everyone.”

The squirrel munched, nerves forgotten. It was not a villain, only a hungry creature who liked delicious food as much as they did, and rather cute besides. They nicknamed it Squeaky, which was only fair.

From that day on, Rafi and Bit always saved extra crumbs for their new friend. The rooftop lunches were still their favorite — food, company, a puzzle solved the delightful way — and Bit kept an extra watchful eye, just in case any other treat decided to vanish. If you ever picnic where the tiles tickle clouds, count your sandwiches twice. Then laugh, and cut a third share anyway.
